text: The manuscript’s strongest organizing contribution is a systematic empirical audit of a second institutional mapping that conventional electoral analysis often leaves implicit. Votes are first translated into seats, and the resulting seat vector is then translated by the legislative majority quota into a weighted majority game and a distribution of a priori pivotal power. Fragmentation characterizes the resulting party configuration, while volatility measures how the electoral inputs and party configuration change across elections. Coalition formation and cabinet instability are downstream political outcomes, but they depend not only on pivotal structure but also on ideological feasibility, party discipline, and bargaining institutions. The manuscript should be reorganized around this hierarchy and should not present the existing evidence as establishing a single and general causal chain from PR to volatility or instability.

text: One plausible organizing sequence is the following. Party-system organization and electoral shocks generate vote distributions; electoral rules translate those vote distributions into seat configurations, while volatility measures changes in electoral support and party supply over time. Majority rule then transforms each seat vector into a distribution of a priori pivotal power. Actual coalition formation and cabinet survival occur downstream, but are conditioned by party discipline, ideological feasibility, bargaining incentives, and external institutional pressures. The manuscript contains evidence relevant to each element, but it does not identify the complete causal sequence. The sequence should therefore organize the descriptive findings.

text: Figure \ref{fig:timeline} shows why the inversion criterion is more demanding than ordinary overrepresentation. Several cabinet coalitions receive a larger share of seats than votes, but only those that cross the Chamber-majority threshold while remaining below the vote-majority threshold count as inversions. In the 2018-linked mandate, the observed coalitions remain below the seat-majority threshold throughout the Bolsonaro period, which explains the absence of inversions despite positive seat differentials in some periods. text: The article fits the special issue by identifying a dark-side mechanism inside proportional representation. It shifts attention from party-level proportionality to coalition-level majority status, showing that post-electoral party sets can command legislative seat majorities without corresponding national vote majorities. The empirical case is Brazil's Chamber of Deputies, where the manuscript studies observed cabinet coalitions and ideologically contiguous party intervals after the 2014, 2018, and 2022 federal-deputy elections.

text: Proportional representation is typically evaluated by asking whether parties receive seats in proportion to votes. In fragmented legislatures, however, the politically relevant unit is often not a party but a coalition. This article examines coalition-level election inversions in Brazil's Chamber of Deputies. A coalition inversion occurs when a set of parties controls a legislative seat majority while receiving less than half of the national federal-deputy vote. Using party vote totals, elected-seat totals, cabinet-period coalition data, and party ideology classifications for the 2014, 2018, and 2022 federal-deputy elections, I identify inversions in two analytically distinct objects: observed cabinet coalitions and ideological intervals defined over the election-year party set. Three observed cabinet periods satisfy the inversion criterion: two during the mandate that followed the 2014 election and one during the mandate that followed the 2022 election. No observed inversion appears after the 2018 election because the relevant cabinet coalitions remain below the Chamber majority threshold. An all-interval ideological search finds minimal connected interval inversions in 2014 and 2022, including a compact  interval with 45.35 percent of the vote and 258 of 513 seats. The results show that Brazil's federally allocated and highly fragmented proportional system can generate coalitional inversions: party sets with less than half of the national vote can nevertheless command legislative majorities.

text: The article fits the special issue by identifying a dark-side mechanism inside proportional representation. It shifts attention from party-level proportionality to coalition-level majority status, showing that post-electoral party sets can command legislative seat majorities without corresponding national vote majorities. The empirical case is Brazil's Chamber of Deputies, where the manuscript studies observed cabinet coalitions and ideologically contiguous party intervals after the 2014, 2018, and 2022 federal-deputy elections.

text: Proportional representation is typically evaluated by asking whether parties receive seats in proportion to votes. In fragmented legislatures, however, the politically relevant unit is often not a party but a coalition. This article examines coalition-level election inversions in Brazil's Chamber of Deputies. A coalition inversion occurs when a set of parties controls a legislative seat majority while receiving less than half of the national federal-deputy vote. Using party vote totals, elected-seat totals, cabinet-period coalition data, and party ideology classifications for the 2014, 2018, and 2022 federal-deputy elections, I identify inversions in two analytically distinct objects: observed cabinet coalitions and ideological intervals defined over the election-year party set. Four observed cabinet periods satisfy the inversion criterion: two during the mandate that followed the 2014 election, one during the mandate that followed the 2018 election, and one during the mandate that followed the 2022 election. The 238-day 2018 case combines 47.25 percent of the vote with exactly 257 seats. An all-interval ideological search finds minimal connected interval inversions in 2014 and 2022, but none in 2018, including a compact 2022 interval with 45.35 percent of the vote and 258 of 513 seats. An accounting decomposition of the four observed inversions shows how their national seat differentials divide into within-district allocation and between-district weighting components. The results show that Brazil's federally allocated and highly fragmented proportional system can generate coalitional inversions: party sets with less than half of the national vote can nevertheless command legislative majorities.

Coalitional presidentialism is dynamic: parties enter and leave the government, changing the set represented in cabinet while the underlying election-year vote and seat distribution remains fixed. These transitions generate successive realized combinations of the same party-level differentials. Cabinet participation is used only to delimit those observable governing party sets. text: These national party seat totals enter a presidential system in which governing capacity ordinarily depends on multiparty arrangements. Brazilian coalitional presidentialism links the presidency to combinations of parties formed across cabinet and Congress: ministries are distributed among several parties, and executive--legislative coordination is organized through agreements among them \parencite{abranches1988presidencialismo,figueiredo2000presidential,pereira2004cost}. The Chamber assembled from twenty-seven district elections therefore supplies the parliamentary resources from which governing coalitions are constructed. Once party seats become inputs into coalition formation, the relevant question is how the positive and negative deviations carried by individual parties behave when those parties are combined.

text: A fragmented legislature permits an enormous number of mathematically possible party subsets. An unrestricted search would be exhaustive, but it would place politically remote combinations on the same footing as combinations that were realized in government or structured by recognizable political proximity. The coalition space is therefore restricted in two different ways. Observed cabinets identify realized governing party combinations. Ideological connectedness supplies a disciplined domain of potential combinations. The two domains answer different questions and should not be treated as alternative measurements of the same object.

text: \subsubsection{Observed cabinet coalitions}

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Cabinet coalitions are substantively meaningful because Brazilian presidents ordinarily govern through multiparty arrangements. Cabinet participation records a party combination that was not merely arithmetically possible but institutionally realized in executive government \parencite{abranches1988presidencialismo,figueiredo2000presidential,pereira2004cost}. The relevant representational question is whether the members of the party set holding ministries collectively possessed a Chamber majority despite receiving less than half of the valid federal-deputy vote in the election that produced that legislature.

text: This domain must be followed across the legislative term rather than fixed at inauguration. Coalitional presidentialism is dynamic: parties enter and leave the government, changing the set represented in cabinet while the underlying election-year vote and seat distribution remains fixed. These transitions generate successive realized combinations of the same party-level differentials. Cabinet participation is used only to delimit those observable governing party sets. It is not treated as a direct vote for a coalition, as an exact measure of legislative voting support, or as evidence that every cabinet party contributes uniformly to congressional coordination.

text: Observed cabinets reveal which combinations entered government, but they cover only a small portion of the majority configurations permitted by the legislature. A systematic analysis of potential coalitional majorities therefore requires a larger domain. Unrestricted enumeration is politically weak, however, because it treats combinations spanning distant parts of the party system as equivalent to combinations whose members occupy a common ideological region. Ideological proximity supplies a theoretically grounded restriction on the coalition space.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Axelrod's connected-coalition criterion provides the baseline restriction: the members of an admissible coalition occupy a contiguous interval in an ideological ordering \parencite{axelrod1970conflict}. Connectedness is not used as a literal model of Brazilian cabinet formation, and it does not imply that ideology predicts which government will form. It provides a conventional way to convert the full combinatorial space into a domain of politically interpretable potential coalitions. Exact connectedness is the baseline because it imposes that restriction in its clearest form.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Exact connectedness is deliberately restrictive. Party locations are estimated rather than known with exact precision, and admissibility can turn on whether a single intermediate party is included. The one-gap domain therefore relaxes the baseline by allowing one party inside the coalition's ideological span to be omitted. This is a narrow robustness test of the no-gap restriction, not a third coalition domain, a behavioral theory of coalition formation, or an unrestricted search. The progression is from realized cabinets to structured potential coalitions and then to a minimal relaxation of the ideological constraint.

text: The empirical construction follows the objects defined above. Election records supply party votes and seats, cabinet records delimit realized coalitions, and party classifications delimit the ideologically constrained potential-coalition domain. Each resulting party set is evaluated by its national vote share, seat total, proportional quota, seat differential, representation ratio, and inversion status.

text: Party labels and electoral allocation units are not identical in every election. In 2014 and 2018, many district seats emerged from joint open lists formed by proportional electoral coalitions. The elected deputies are subsequently attributed to their member parties, allowing national party vote totals, seat totals, quotas, and differentials to be constructed even though the member parties did not receive separate within-coalition seat allocations. In 2022, federations pooled member-party votes and candidates for electoral allocation. Member-party vote and seat totals are retained because cabinet participation and ideological classifications are observed at the party level. Section~\ref{sec:brazil-system} supplies the institutional details; here the distinction serves only to connect the electoral records to the party-level quantities used in the coalition analysis.

text: Cabinet coalitions are substantively meaningful because Brazilian presidents ordinarily govern through multiparty arrangements. Cabinet participation records a party combination that was not merely arithmetically possible but institutionally realized in executive government \parencite{abranches1988presidencialismo,figueiredo2000presidential,pereira2004cost}. text: This domain must be followed across the legislative term. Coalitional presidentialism is dynamic: parties enter and leave the government, changing the set represented in cabinet while the underlying election-year vote and seat distribution remains fixed. These transitions generate successive realized combinations of the same party-level differentials. Cabinet participation is used only to delimit those observable governing party sets. This provides a useful setting for studying coalition inversion because changes in inversion status can occur without any change in the underlying electoral result: what changes is the particular combination of parties across which the fixed vote-seat differentials are aggregated. The cabinet sequence therefore reveals whether, and for how long, politically realized recombinations of the same legislature cross the majority threshold without a corresponding vote majority.

text: The article fits the special issue by identifying a dark-side mechanism inside proportional representation. It shifts attention from party-level proportionality to coalition-level majority status, showing that post-electoral party sets can command legislative seat majorities without corresponding national vote majorities. The empirical case is Brazil's Chamber of Deputies, where the manuscript studies observed cabinet coalitions and ideologically contiguous party intervals after the 2014, 2018, and 2022 federal-deputy elections.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Proportional representation is typically evaluated by asking whether parties receive seats in proportion to votes. In fragmented legislatures, however, the politically relevant unit is often not a party but a coalition. This article examines coalition-level election inversions in Brazil's Chamber of Deputies. A coalition inversion occurs when a set of parties controls a legislative seat majority while receiving less than half of the national federal-deputy vote. Using party vote totals, elected-seat totals, cabinet-period coalition data, and party ideology classifications for the 2014, 2018, and 2022 federal-deputy elections, I identify inversions in two analytically distinct objects: observed cabinet coalitions and ideological intervals defined over the election-year party set. Four observed cabinet periods satisfy the inversion criterion: two during the mandate that followed the 2014 election, one during the mandate that followed the 2018 election, and one during the mandate that followed the 2022 election. The 238-day 2018 case combines 47.25 percent of the vote with exactly 257 seats. An all-interval ideological search finds minimal connected interval inversions in 2014 and 2022, but none in 2018, including a compact 2022 interval with 45.35 percent of the vote and 258 of 513 seats. An accounting decomposition of the four observed inversions shows how their national seat differentials divide into within-district allocation and between-district weighting components. The results show that Brazil's federally allocated and highly fragmented proportional system can generate coalitional inversions: party sets with less than half of the national vote can nevertheless command legislative majorities.

text: Cabinet coalitions are substantively meaningful because Brazilian presidents ordinarily govern through multiparty arrangements. text: This domain must be followed across the legislative term. Coalitional presidentialism is dynamic: parties enter and leave the government, changing the set represented in cabinet while the underlying election-year vote and seat distribution remains fixed. These transitions generate successive realized combinations of the same party-level differentials. Cabinet participation is used only to delimit those observable governing party sets. This provides a useful setting for studying coalition inversion because changes in inversion status can occur without any change in the underlying electoral result: what changes is the particular combination of parties across which the fixed vote-seat differentials are aggregated. The cabinet sequence therefore reveals whether, and for how long, politically realized recombinations of the same legislature cross the majority threshold without a corresponding vote majority.

text: These national party seat totals enter a presidential system in which governing capacity ordinarily depends on multiparty arrangements. Brazilian coalitional presidentialism links the presidency to combinations of parties formed across cabinet and Congress: ministries are distributed among several parties, and executive--legislative coordination is organized through agreements among them \parencite{abranches1988presidencialismo,figueiredo2000presidential,pereira2004cost}. The Chamber assembled from twenty-seven district elections therefore supplies the parliamentary resources from which governing coalitions are constructed. Once party seats become inputs into coalition formation, the relevant question is how the positive and negative deviations carried by individual parties behave when those parties are combined.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: A fragmented legislature permits an enormous number of mathematically possible party subsets. An unrestricted search would be exhaustive, but it would place politically remote combinations on the same footing as combinations that were realized in government or structured by recognizable political proximity. The coalition space is therefore restricted in two different ways. Observed cabinets identify realized governing party combinations. Ideological connectedness supplies a disciplined domain of potential combinations. The two domains answer different questions and should not be treated as alternative measurements of the same object.

text: \subsubsection{Observed cabinet coalitions}

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Cabinet coalitions are substantively meaningful because Brazilian presidents ordinarily govern through multiparty arrangements. Cabinet participation records a party combination that was not merely arithmetically possible but institutionally realized in executive government \parencite{abranches1988presidencialismo,figueiredo2000presidential,pereira2004cost}. The relevant representational question is whether the members of the party set holding ministries collectively possessed a Chamber majority despite receiving less than half of the valid federal-deputy vote in the election that produced that legislature.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: This domain must be followed across the legislative term rather than fixed at inauguration. Coalitional presidentialism is dynamic: parties enter and leave the government, changing the set represented in cabinet while the underlying election-year vote and seat distribution remains fixed. These transitions generate successive realized combinations of the same party-level differentials. Cabinet participation is used only to delimit those observable governing party sets. It is not treated as a direct vote for a coalition, as an exact measure of legislative voting support, or as evidence that every cabinet party contributes uniformly to congressional coordination.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Observed cabinets reveal which combinations entered government, but they cover only a small portion of the majority configurations permitted by the legislature. A systematic analysis of potential coalitional majorities therefore requires a larger domain. Unrestricted enumeration is politically weak, however, because it treats combinations spanning distant parts of the party system as equivalent to combinations whose members occupy a common ideological region. Ideological proximity supplies a theoretically grounded restriction on the coalition space.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Axelrod's connected-coalition criterion provides the baseline restriction: the members of an admissible coalition occupy a contiguous interval in an ideological ordering \parencite{axelrod1970conflict}. Connectedness is not used as a literal model of Brazilian cabinet formation, and it does not imply that ideology predicts which government will form. It provides a conventional way to convert the full combinatorial space into a domain of politically interpretable potential coalitions. Exact connectedness is the baseline because it imposes that restriction in its clearest form.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Exact connectedness is deliberately restrictive. Party locations are estimated rather than known with exact precision, and admissibility can turn on whether a single intermediate party is included. The one-gap domain therefore relaxes the baseline by allowing one party inside the coalition's ideological span to be omitted. This is a narrow robustness test of the no-gap restriction, not a third coalition domain, a behavioral theory of coalition formation, or an unrestricted search. The progression is from realized cabinets to structured potential coalitions and then to a minimal relaxation of the ideological constraint.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: The empirical construction follows the objects defined above. Election records supply party votes and seats, cabinet records delimit realized coalitions, and party classifications delimit the ideologically constrained potential-coalition domain. Each resulting party set is evaluated by its national vote share, seat total, proportional quota, seat differential, representation ratio, and inversion status.

role: other draft, report or archived source
text: Party labels and electoral allocation units are not identical in every election. In 2014 and 2018, many district seats emerged from joint open lists formed by proportional electoral coalitions. The elected deputies are subsequently attributed to their member parties, allowing national party vote totals, seat totals, quotas, and differentials to be constructed even though the member parties did not receive separate within-coalition seat allocations. In 2022, federations pooled member-party votes and candidates for electoral allocation. Member-party vote and seat totals are retained because cabinet participation and ideological classifications are observed at the party level. Section~\ref{sec:brazil-system} supplies the institutional details; here the distinction serves only to connect the electoral records to the party-level quantities used in the coalition analysis.

text: Cabinet composition is reconstructed from the Brazilian Wikipedia cabinet-member lists for the Dilma Rousseff, Michel Temer, Jair Bolsonaro, and Lula III administrations. The appointment records identify the office, incumbent, party label, entry date, and exit date. A cabinet period is defined as an interval during which the set of parties holding ministries or ministry-level offices remains unchanged. A party's entry or exit begins a new period, even when the corresponding election-year vote and seat vector remains the same.

text: The 2014 election is linked to cabinet periods from January 1, 2015 through December 31, 2018; the 2018 election to periods from January 1, 2019 through December 31, 2022; and the 2022 election to the observed Lula III period from January 1, 2023 through March 19, 2026. Cabinet labels are harmonized and translated to the party labels used in the election that produced the corresponding Chamber delegation. Coalition votes and seats are then obtained by summing the election-year party totals for the cabinet party set. One-to-one renames, party fusions, and the complete translation tables remain documented in the replication materials.\footnote{Further implementation details are available in the replication repository: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/electoral-inversion-B6B5/README.md}.}
